newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Another S.Korean steel firm in trouble, stocks hit.
newsitem.headline: Another S.Korean steel firm in trouble, stocks hit.

text.p: Another South Korean steel company has filed for court receivership, dealing a new blow to the ailing banking system and raising fears of more corporate failures.
Sammi Steel Co sought protection from its creditors on Tuesday along with four other affiliates of Sammi Group, one of South Korea's top 30 business conglomerates.
It was the second steel maker to founder this year.
The news sent share prices on the Seoul stock exchange tumbling on Wednesday to 644.72, down 2.01 percent or 13.25 points, in early afternoon trading. Banking and securities shares led the slide.
In January, Hanbo Steel Co filed for receivership under debts of $5.8 billion in South Korea's biggest corporate collapse.
Hanbo is the country's second largest steelmaker after Pohang Iron and Steel Co (POSCO).
"There is a good possibility of further bankruptcies coming on line," said Lim Chun-soo, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd.

Korea First Bank is Sammi Steel's biggest creditor, with 395.9 billion won ($448.6 million) of outstanding loans at the end of 1996. The bank issued a statement saying it would seek a buyer for the stricken firm.
Korea First is also the biggest lender to Hanbo Steel. Last month its long-term rating was lowered by Moody's Investors Service.
Sammi Steel had liabilities of 1.45 trillion won ($1.6 billion) at the end of 1996 against assets of 1.53 trillion won, according to company figures.

It has been reeling under the weight of debt repayments, aggravated by falling prices for its stainless steel products. In calendar 1996 it posted a net loss of 119.98 billion won against a loss of 39.45 billion in 1995.
Trading in shares of Sammi Steel and its marketing affiliate Sammi Corp was halted.
Sammi Metal Products Co, Sammi Technology and Industries Co and Sammi Fine Ceramics Co -- the other troubled units of Sammi Group -- are not listed.
At a news conference, Sammi group chairman Kim Hyun-bae said he was confident the group would recover after selling real estate and other assets.
"I am confident we will achieve business normalisation in a fairly short period of time," he said.
Kim said real estate sales would take time to complete. In the meantime, the group could not handle rising financing costs and faced difficulty securing fresh loans.

South Korea's banking system was shaken by the Hanbo failure, which exposed weak credit analysis and corrupt lending practices. Three top bankers are now on trial for bribery in a loans scandal linked to the collapse.
As a result of the scandal, South Korean banks are paying more for overseas loans.
Sammi's woes might further squeeze already tight credit to struggling small and medium-sized companies, said Kim Myung-ho, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
"Banks will be more conservative in loans," he said.

Kim said he did not expect Sammi Steel would have much difficulty obtaining court protection, which would allow it to restructure. He said the firm's troubles stemmed mainly from a cyclical business downturn, not management faults.
Last month Sammi Steel sold part of its speciality iron rod production business to POSCO in a deal valued at 719.4 billion won. Full payment was due during the first half of this year.
Sammi has stainless steel operations in Canada and the United States.
